label: Number of Faces in Arrangements
notes: This chapter, spanning printed pages 125 to 164, asks a deceptively simple question: how many faces does an arrangement of hyperplanes carry. We meet vertices, edges, and cells of every dimension, the zone theorem bounding faces near one hyperplane, levels, and the incidence applications these counts power.

label: Arrangements of Hyperplanes
notes: An arrangement is the dissection of space produced by a finite family of hyperplanes. Each hyperplane splits everything into two open halfspaces, and intersecting all the resulting regions gives the faces. Faces range in dimension from zero, the vertices, up to the full ambient dimension, the cells.

label: Faces of Every Dimension
notes: A k-face is a maximal connected piece of space whose points lie on the same chosen subset of hyperplanes and the same side of the rest. We total all faces across dimensions zero through d. This grand total is the combinatorial complexity that the chapter learns to bound sharply.

label: Simple Arrangements
notes: An arrangement is simple when no d plus one hyperplanes share a point and every d of them meet in exactly one vertex. Simplicity makes the face counts extremal: simple arrangements maximize vertices, so any bound proved for them governs the general degenerate case too.

label: Counting in the Plane
notes: For n lines in general position the plane is cut into vertices, edges, and cells. Choosing pairs gives the vertices, an Euler relation then fixes edges and cells. All three counts grow quadratically, confirming the plane arrangement has complexity on the order of n squared.

label: Total Complexity Theta(n^d)
notes: In d dimensions a simple arrangement of n hyperplanes has faces of each dimension counted by binomial sums in n. Summing over all dimensions, the total number of faces is Theta of n to the d. This polynomial blow-up is both an upper bound and, for simple families, exactly attained.

label: The Zone of a Hyperplane
notes: The zone of a hyperplane h is the collection of all faces of the arrangement that touch h, meaning faces whose closure meets h. Visually it is the corridor of cells that h passes through together with their boundary pieces. Its size is far smaller than the whole arrangement.

label: The Zone Theorem
notes: The zone theorem states that the total complexity of all faces in the zone of a single hyperplane is O of n to the d minus one. Despite a cell having many faces, summed over the entire zone the count stays one order below the full arrangement. The proof uses clever charging.

label: Proof Idea: Induction and Charging
notes: The standard proof removes one hyperplane, applies the bound inductively, then reinserts it and charges the newly created zone faces to the faces they split. A careful left-right accounting ensures each face is charged a bounded number of times, yielding the linear-in-the-codimension constant.

label: Levels and the k-Level
notes: Given lines in the plane, the level of a point is the number of lines strictly below it. The k-level is the closure of all arrangement edges whose level equals k. Bounding the complexity of a single level is a famously hard open problem, far subtler than the full count.

label: Many Cells and Incidences
notes: Face counts feed incidence geometry. Bounding how many cells can be rich, touching many lines, or how many point-line incidences m points and n lines admit, reduces to arrangement complexity. The Szemeredi-Trotter bound and the many-cells theorem are the headline applications of these counting tools.

label: Recap and Toolkit
notes: We assembled a counting toolkit: faces of all dimensions total Theta n to the d, simplicity makes this extremal, the zone theorem caps faces near one hyperplane at O of n to the d minus one, levels remain hard, and incidence bounds inherit all of this. These are foundations for cuttings and range searching.
